newsitem.title: PERU: Explosions give way to toasts as Peru crisis ends.
newsitem.headline: Explosions give way to toasts as Peru crisis ends.

text.p: Two hours after bombs and bullets ended Latin America's longest hostage siege, the sound of laughter and chink of glasses being raised in triumph could be heard at Peru's emergency military command centre.
Security heads were celebrating the successful end to a daring operation that rescued 71 hostages who had been held since December at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.
"We always knew that we could do it," one policeman said as he mopped sweat from his brow. "We've been preparing for this for a long time. Now we can all go home."
Tuesday had seemed just another routine day at the residence.

Red Cross workers took in food and drink for the 72 hostages held by Marxist rebels. Journalists surrounding the site expected, at most, the arrival of one or all of three negotiators trying to bring a peaceful end to the standoff.
Then two loud explosions and a burst of gunfire broke the tedium.
Within seconds the word was out. "They're going in," shouted panicked passersby running away from, and journalists rushing toward, the residence.
Further explosions followed and dozens of troops were seen swarming into the diplomatic compound and surrounding the building.

As smoke billowed into the sky, the first hostages began to emerge from an upper window of the residence. Guided by troops wearing ski-masks, they crawled across a roof on their hands and knees as the bullets flew around their heads. The sudden attack caught some hostages half-dressed.
Compared to the clinical military operation taking place at the residence, the scene in the nearby streets was chaotic.
At one street corner about a block and a half from the residence, police officers and army troops nearly came to blows as the entrance of dozens of ambulances was blocked.
Distraught family members stood nearby, shaking with tears and desperate for information.
"You people never know anything, damn it," one man shouted at a policeman after his inquiry over the safety of the captives was rebuffed.

Then the news began to trickle out. All but one hostage had been freed; all 14 of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels were dead; President Alberto Fujimori had arrived at the site; the MRTA flag had been pulled down; and victorious troops were singing the national anthem on the roof of the residence.
When the two buses carrying palid but relieved-looking hostages swept out, the 40-minute battle was nearly over.
Crowds lining the route cheered, but the hostages appeared too shell-shocked to raise an arm in recognition.
Flames climbed into the air from the rear of the mansion and explosions continued to thunder from the interior.
But the atmosphere had changed to one of quiet jubilation.

Fujimori, the man of the moment, arrived again. His cavalcade ground to a halt under the weight of journalists and onlookers and he made his first public comments on the storming standing on the roof of his car.
Dressed in a bullet-proof waistcoat, Fujimori's voice trembled and tears welled in his eyes as he gave news that one hostage and two officers had been killed in the attack.
"Long live Peru!" someone shouted from the crowd.
